blocks.text: Acts 2 narrates Pentecost in Jerusalem during a major pilgrimage feast when devout Jews from many nations have gathered. The apostles are together in one place when a rushing wind fills the house where they sit, and fiery appearances distribute themselves among them. Those present speak in other tongues as the Spirit gives them utterance—a moment the narrative presents as foundational to the early church's self-understanding.

sections.title: The Multilingual Phenomenon and Crowd Reaction

blocks.text: When the sound is heard, a crowd gathers and experiences confusion because each person hears the apostles speaking in their own native language. Acts lists representatives from a remarkable span of the diaspora: Parthians, Medes, and Elamites from the eastern reaches; residents of Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, and the provinces of Asia; people from Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; sojourners from Rome; Cretans and Arabians. This geographical sweep underscores the scale of pilgrimage to Jerusalem for the feast.

The crowd's reaction splits. Some are amazed and marveled, asking 'What does this mean?' Others mock, claiming the apostles are filled with new wine. Acts depicts recognizable diaspora languages at Pentecost while the precise relation to other early Christian speech phenomena remains debated. The account preserves an intelligible multilingual scene—each native hearer understands in their own language—and this framing should not be conflated with other descriptions of Spirit-induced utterance elsewhere in early Christian sources.

sections.title: Peter's Speech and the Joel Quotation

blocks.text: Peter stands with the eleven and addresses the crowd, defending the apostles against the drunkenness charge by noting it is only the third hour of the day. He then interprets the event through prophecy: 'This is what was spoken through the prophet Joel.' Peter explicitly quotes and adapts the Old Greek Joel text, beginning with 'In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.' This citation connects the immediate Pentecost event to Joel's prophetic vision and establishes a hermeneutical frame for understanding the Spirit-empowered moment.

Acts' speeches are literary compositions within ancient narrative and cannot be treated as stenographic transcripts, though they may preserve earlier traditions. Peter's address therefore represents Luke's narrative interpretation and theological framing of the Pentecost moment rather than a verbatim record of what was spoken.

Peter emerges as a leading voice in the early Jerusalem community. A fisherman from Galilee, he becomes a prominent witness in Jesus' ministry and the church. The Pentecost narrative presents tongues-speaking as part of Spirit reception. However, Acts describes Spirit reception across different scenes with varying sequences and particular signs. This variability is significant: the absence of one sign in a given scene should not be read as proof that a group was excluded from Spirit reception.

Acts 2 is preserved in early papyri and major Greek codices, including P45, P53, and P74, along with the uncial manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae. These witnesses contribute different portions and textual profiles. Codex Bezae and related versional traditions preserve a substantially distinctive text of Acts often called the Western text, whose individual readings require case-by-case judgment. Historical evaluation of Acts must compare particular claims with independent evidence rather than assign blanket reliability or unreliability to the entire narrative.
